2.text: are told of experiences in harnessing young wolves. One Russianized Yukaghir

3.text: told me that his own grandfather tried to harness tame wolves, but that they

4.text: proved useless. They were too shy, and would frequently lie down flat and

5.text: allow themselves to be dragged by the team. Moreover, the amount of food

6.text: required by them daily was three times as much as is needed by the dog.

7.text: According to the belief of the Russianized natives of the Kolyma, the “forest-

8.text: owner,” a supernatural being,¹ drives, instead of dogs, foxes and wolves.

9.text: Perhaps this belief accounts for the amplification of the above story.

10.text: Among the Chukchee and the Koryak the dog is also used for sacrifice,

11.text: and even for food. The Maritime Koryak sacrifice so many dogs, that not

12.text: enough are left for driving. The Reindeer Chukchee sacrifice both reindeer

13.text: and dogs frequently, but the poorer people sacrifice principally dogs and puppies.

14.text: Besides this, the Maritime Chukchee and the Eskimo use dogs for food in

15.text: case of famine. In the winter of 1901, for instance, the Chukchee families

16.text: of Mariinsky Post, at the mouth of the Anadyr, suffered greatly from famine,

17.text: and ate nearly all their dogs. I know of cases where families of the Arctic

18.text: shore have, in times of famine, eaten all their dogs. Even in times of plenty,

19.text: some families occasionally kill a fat dog to feast on its head and intestines,

20.text: although, on account of the jeers of Russian cossacks and American whalers,

21.text: that taste has decreased rapidly, or at least its gratification is concealed from

22.text: other people. However, when I wanted specimens of dog-skin, the natives

23.text: who killed the animals for me were careful to take the meat home for their.

27.text: It is not necessary to speak of the races of the East Siberian team-dog,

28.text: since all dogs are much alike in size and color. On an average, they are

29.text: of the size of an ordinary shepherd-dog; rather smaller, however, than the

30.text: dogs of the American Eskimo. Their appearance calls to mind the wolf; and

31.text: the form of their heads, the jackal. They are shaggy, and have very thick,

32.text: woolly tails, especially in the more exposed regions along the seacoast. Among

33.text: the Yakut on the Upper Kolyma I have often met dogs of curious appearance,

34.text: resembling that of the fox. They were undersized, with rather long bodies

37.text: The most frequent colors of team-dogs are brindle wolf, black, white,

39.text: last two chiefly on the Pacific side); in southern Kamchatka they are some-
